Liu Ban remarked: "In my opinion, halting the Yellow River breach and erecting the Longyuan Palace were two distinct events; the construction of the palace was not undertaken simply on account of repairing the river breach. Yan Shigu suspected that it ought to say Longyuan Shrine; yet according to the Annals of Emperor Jing, when the Deyang Shrine was established, it was also referred to as the Deyang Palace. How could one ever claim that it was not the Deyang Shrine? This Longyuan Palace should indeed be as stated in the Sanfu Huangtu."

In the fourth year, in winter, Dou Ying, the Marquis of Weiqi, was found guilty of a crime and executed in the public marketplace.

<note>Yan Shigu noted: "This was because he had formed a faction with Guan Fu."</note>

In spring, in the third month, on the day <term>yimao</term> <gloss>day 52 of the sexagenary cycle</gloss>, Chancellor Tian Fen died. In summer, in the fourth month, frost fell and killed the grasses. In the fifth month, an earthquake occurred. An amnesty was granted to all under Heaven.

In the fifth year, in spring, in the first month, Liu De, King of Hejian, died. In summer, troops were dispatched from Ba and Shu to construct the road to the Southern Barbarians. In addition, ten thousand soldiers were mobilized to fortify and open the strategic defiles of Yanmen.

<note>Yan Shigu noted: "This was done to strengthen defenses in order to halt the incursions of the Xiongnu." Liu Ban remarked: "In my opinion, repairing the strategic defiles meant opening the roads to make them level and easy to traverse, solely to facilitate launching campaigns against the Xiongnu."</note>

In autumn, in the seventh month, a great gale uprooted trees. On the day <term>yisi</term> <gloss>day 42 of the sexagenary cycle</gloss>, Empress Chen was deposed, and those who practiced witchcraft were arrested.

<summary>Yan Shigu and Liu Ban comment on the location of Longyuan Palace, after which Dou Ying is executed, Chancellor Tian Fen dies, King Liu De passes away, military roads and passes are fortified against the Xiongnu, and Empress Chen is deposed amid witchcraft investigations.</summary>

In the first month, on the day <term>wuzi</term>, a fire broke out at the Yangling Mausoleum Park. In summer, in the fourth month, it hailed.

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "The character for rain or hail falling <term>yu</term> is pronounced with the fanqie phonetic of yu and ju inverted."</note>

More than ten commanderies and kingdoms east of Hangu Pass suffered famine, and people ate one another. Shun, King of Changshan, died; his son Dun succeeded to the throne, but committed a crime, was deposed, and was banished to Fangling.

In the fourth year <note>113 BCE</note>, in winter, in the tenth month, the Emperor traveled to Yong to sacrifice at the Five Altars. He bestowed one rank of nobility upon each male head of household, and one hundred families of women were granted an ox and wine. He proceeded from Xiayang, traveling east to visit Fenyin.

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "Xiayang is a county of Fengyi. Fenyin belongs to Hedong. The character Fen is pronounced with the fanqie phonetic of fu and yun inverted."</note>

In the eleventh month, on the day <term>jiazi</term>, an altar to the <term>Houtu</term> <gloss>Earth Goddess</gloss> was established on the bank of the Fen River at <term>Chui</term>.

<note>Su Lin stated: "The character Chui is pronounced shui."</note>

<note>Ru Chun stated: "Chui refers to a mound rising abruptly on the east bank of the Yellow River, four or five li long, over two li wide, and more than a hundred feet high. The county seat of Fenyin was governed atop the Chui mound. The altar to Houtu lies west of the county. The Fen River lies north of the Chui mound and flows west to merge with the Yellow River."</note>

<note>Yan Shigu stated: "Both explanations are correct. Chui takes its name from its high, bulging shape resembling a person's buttocks and rump. Another explanation is that this place overlooked the Fen River and was originally named Lin, which sounds the same as kui. The local people pronounced kui like shui, which caused the name to shift."</note>

<summary>This page records portents and natural disasters including a fire at Yangling and severe famine east of the pass leading to cannibalism, followed by Emperor Wu's imperial tour to Yong, his sacrifices at the Five Altars, and the establishment of the imperial altar to the Earth Goddess Houtu at Chui in Fenyin.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>He then dispatched an envoy to persuade him. The Chanyu's envoy arrived but died at the capital. The Xiongnu raided the border, so General Who Plucks the Hu Guo Chang was dispatched to garrison Shuofang.

In the winter of the fifth year <note>106 BCE</note>, the Emperor embarked on an inspection tour southward, arriving at Shengtang.

<note>Wen Ying stated: "According to the 'Treatise on Geography,' there is no such county name. I suspect it should be located near Lujiang." Wei Zhao stated: "It is located in Nanjun." Yan Shigu stated: "Wei's explanation is correct."</note>

From afar, he offered sacrifice to Shun of Yu at Mount Jiuyi.

<note>Ying Shao stated: "Shun was buried at Cangwu. Jiuyi is the name of a mountain, now located in Yingdao of Lingling." Wen Ying stated: "Mount Jiuyi lies half in Cangwu and half in Lingling." Ru Chun stated: "Shun was buried at Jiuyi, and Jiuyi is located in Fengcheng County of Cangwu; hence it is sometimes said that Shun was buried at Cangwu." Yan Shigu stated: "Wen's explanation is correct. The character <term>yi</term> <gloss>嶷</gloss> is pronounced like <term>yi</term> <gloss>疑, doubt</gloss>. The mountain has nine peaks whose forms and appearances closely resemble one another, which is why it is called Mount Jiuyi <gloss>Nine Doubts Mountain</gloss>." Song Qi stated: "In old editions, after 'is correct' there was the character 'Nine,' and beneath 'yi' there was no pronunciation gloss for 'yi.' The text was corrected according to the Imperial History Office edition."</note>

He climbed Mount Tianzhu in Qian.

<note>Ying Shao stated: "The character <term>qian</term> <gloss>灊</gloss> is pronounced like <term>qian</term> <gloss>潛, submerged</gloss>. Mount Huo, the Southern Sacred Peak, is located in Qian. Qian is the name of a county belonging to Lujiang." Wen Ying stated: "Mount Tianzhu is in the south of Qian County, where a shrine is situated. The character <term>qian</term> is pronounced <term>cen</term>." Yan Shigu stated: "The character <term>qian</term> is pronounced the same as <term>qian</term> <gloss>潛</gloss>. Ying's explanation is correct."</note>

From Xunyang, he floated down the Yangtze River and shot a river dragon with his own hands in the midst of the river, capturing it.

<summary>Emperor Wu dispatches Guo Chang to defend Shuofang against Xiongnu incursions, conducts an imperial progress southward to Shengtang, performs distant sacrifices to Emperor Shun at Mount Jiuyi, ascends Mount Tianzhu in Qian, and personally hunts a river dragon while sailing on the Yangtze River from Xunyang.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>When the Emperor heard of it, he took pity on him, established Luan as King of Sishui, and had the Chancellor and Senior Scribe cast into prison. In the third month, silk fabric was bestowed upon those selected by the commanderies and kingdoms for conduct and righteousness, including Han Fu of Zhuo Commandery and four others, fifty bolts per person, and they were sent home. An edict declared: "We regret to wear them out with the burdens of official duties."

<note>Deng Zhan states: "The Emperor took pity and felt grief for Han Fu and the others, and could not bear to wear them out with labor and service in official duties."</note>

"Let them devote themselves to cultivating filial piety and brotherly respect in order to instruct their local communities. Let the commanderies and counties regularly grant them sheep and wine in the first month. If any among them meets with misfortune, grant them a single suit of clothing and quilts, and sacrifice to them with a <term>zhonglao</term> <gloss>secondary sacrificial offering of sheep and pig</gloss>."

<note>Yan Shigu states: "Fortunate means auspicious and avoiding misfortune; hence death is referred to as misfortune. A suit refers to a complete set, like saying a pair or set today. The <term>zhonglao</term> is the lesser offering <term>shaolao</term>, referring to a sheep and a pig."</note>

The Di people of Wudu rebelled.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The character <term>Di</term> has the fanqie pronunciation of <term>ding</term> and <term>xi</term>."</note>

The Commander of the Capital Gendarmes <term>Zhi Jinwu</term> Ma Shi Jian and Marquis of Long'e Han Zeng were dispatched.

<note>Yan Shigu states: "The surname was Mashi and the personal name was Jian. For Long'e, editions of the Hanshu sometimes write the character <term>Luo</term>. The Table of Meritorious Officials and Marquises states that Han Tuodang, Marquis Zhuang of Gonggao, had a son named Gui who was enfeoffed as Marquis of Longluo. In the fifth year of the Yuanding era he was stripped of rank due to the gold offering offense. In the first year of the Houyuan era, Gui's younger brother's son Zeng succeeded to the enfeoffment as Marquis of Longluo. Xun Yue's Han Annals uses the character <term>E</term> for all instances of Longluo. Cui Hao says that <term>luo</term> is pronounced like <term>luo</term>."</note>

<note>Former Han Annals commentary by Ciding: "...serving others has three grades..."</note>

<summary>Emperor Zhao restores the Kingdom of Sishui for the posthumous prince Luan, punishes negligent officials, rewards virtuous elders with stipends, and dispatches generals to quell a Di rebellion in Wudu.</summary>

From this, Hu Jian became famous. Later, he served as Magistrate of Weicheng <note>original: "渭城令"</note>, where his governance earned great renown. It happened that Emperor Zhao was young, and General Shangguan An, father of the Empress, was on friendly terms with Ding Wairen, the paramour of the Emperor's elder sister, the Eldest Princess Gai. Ding Wairen was arrogant and unrestrained; bearing a grudge against Fan Fu, the former Intendant of the Capital, he sent a retainer to shoot and kill him. The retainer hid in the residence of the Princess, and the magistrates dared not arrest him. Hu Jian, Magistrate of Weicheng, led officers and soldiers to surround and arrest him. When Princess Gai heard of it, she, Ding Wairen, and General Shangguan went with a large entourage of slaves and retainers, rushing on horseback and shooting at the pursuing officers. <note>Yan Shigu states: "*Ben* </note><note>original: '犇'</note> is an ancient form of *ben* <note>original: '奔'</note>, meaning running forward in haste to shoot."

The officers scattered and fled. Princess Gai sent an archer-attendant to indict the Weicheng patrol officer for injuring slaves of the Princess's household. Hu Jian reported that there was no other crime committed. <note>Fu Qian states: "This means the patrol officer was performing public duty and had committed no other crime." Liu Ban states: "The character *ling* <gloss>magistrate</gloss> is superfluous here."</note>

In the way of loving relatives, preserving them whole is foremost. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "Striving to preserve them in security and peace is the highest priority."</note> One ought to grant them worthy teachers and good tutors to instruct them in the way of loyalty and filial piety. Yet now they are honored and doted upon in high positions, and entrusted with supreme authority <note>Yan Shigu comments: "This uses the Big Dipper constellation as an analogy: the body of the Dipper is the bowl, while the handle controls direction. Giving them the handle means granting executive power."</note>, causing them to become arrogant and rebellious until they are exterminated. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "'Yi' means to level, referring to wiping them out completely."</note> This is the greatest failure in loving relatives. Even a man of Huo Guang's worthiness could not plan for his descendants; therefore, when powerful ministers pass authority to the next generation, danger inevitably follows.

The Classic of History says: "Do not let it be like a fire that starts small and faint." <note>Yan Shigu comments: "These are words from the 'Luo Announcement' <term>Luo gao</term> in the Book of Zhou <term>Zhou shu</term>. 'Yongyong' describes something minute and faint. It means that if a fire begins small and is not extinguished early, it will blaze up fiercely. When high ministers monopolize power, one must likewise plan early to strip them of their authority."</note> When their power overawes the sovereign and their authority surpasses that of the ruler, attempting to prevent disaster afterward will be too late. <note>Yan Shigu comments: "'Yi' is a final particle marking the conclusion of the statement."</note>

### Scroll Sixty-Eight

In that month, Huo Guang's brother-in-law, Palace Attendant and Grand Palace Grandee Zhang Shuo, was also sent out to serve as Grand Administrator of Shu Commandery. His granddaughter's husband, General of the Household Wang Han, was appointed Grand Administrator of Wuwei. Soon after, he again reassigned Huo Guang's eldest daughter's husband, Commandant of the Guards of the Changle Palace Deng Guanghan, to serve as Privy Purse. 

He further appointed Huo Yu as Commander-in-Chief, wearing a small cap without seal and ribbons, and dismissed his right-flank garrison command and subordinate officials. The purpose of giving Huo Yu the official title of Commander-in-Chief alongside Huo Guang was specifically to disarm his authority.

<gloss>Su Lin says: "<term>Te</term> <gloss>specifically</gloss> means merely." By the beginning of the Benshi reign <note>73–70 BCE</note>, the Xiongnu harbored treacherous and recalcitrant ambitions.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Jie</term> <gloss>obstinate/stubborn</gloss> means hard and rebellious. It signifies that they arose in disobedience.</note>

They wished to plunder the Wusun and violate the Han princess. Thereupon, five generals were dispatched leading an expeditionary army of 150,000 cavalry to hunt down the enemy across the south, while the Marquis of Changluo led 50,000 cavalry from the Wusun to strike awe throughout their western border. Both forces reached their agreed rendezvous points and returned.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>pledge/rendezvous</gloss> means good faith; it refers to the appointed place.</note>

At that time, they captured little.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Xian</term> <gloss>rare</gloss> means few; it is pronounced like <term>xian</term> combined with <term>jian</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

They merely displayed their martial prowess and manifested the might of Han forces like thunder and wind. Although they marched out and returned empty-handed, two generals were nevertheless executed for their failures. Therefore, the northern barbarians did not submit, and the Central Plains could not yet rest easy on high pillows.

When it came to the Yuankang and Shenjue eras <note>65–58 BCE</note>, great spiritual virtue and majestic grace spread widely, while internal turmoil erupted within the Xiongnu. Five Chanyu competed for the throne. Rizhu and Huhanye brought their state to submit in desperation, prostrating themselves and declaring themselves subjects.

<note>Yan Shigu says: <term>Fu</term> <gloss>prostrate</gloss> is pronounced like <term>pu</term> combined with <term>bei</term> <gloss>fan</gloss>.</note>

Yet the Han court still maintained the strategy of loose rein <note>jimi</note>, not assuming arbitrary and total control over them.

<note>Yan Shigu says: The character <term>zhuan</term> is identical with <term>zhuan</term> <gloss>monopolize/dominate</gloss>. <term>Zhuanzhi</term> <gloss>exclusive control</gloss> refers to reducing them completely to subjects and bondservants.</note>

<summary>Following minor frontier campaigns against the Xiongnu during the Benshi reign, internal civil war fractured the Xiongnu under five rival Chanyu, prompting Huhanye to submit to Han authority under the loose-rein policy.</summary>

Ying Shao stated: "<term>Hong</term> <gloss>red/coarse cloth</gloss> refers to using red cloth for the collars and borders during the intermediate sacrifice of auspiciousness and the great sacrifice of auspiciousness. <term>Xian</term> <gloss>fine hemp</gloss> means unlined garments. In total, thirty-six days elapse before shedding mourning garments; this represents substituting days for months." Jin Zhuo stated: "It is standard practice in the Book of Han to use <term>hong</term> <gloss>red</gloss> in place of <term>gong</term> <gloss>coarse mourning cloth</gloss>." Yan Shigu stated: "<term>Hong</term> <gloss>red</gloss> and <term>gong</term> <gloss>coarse mourning cloth</gloss> are identical; the two explanations of Fu and Jin are correct. This mourning regulation was created by Emperor Wen following his own personal judgment; it was not derived from the Rites of Zhou. Why should it be regarded as substituting days for months? The three-year mourning period in fact spans twenty-seven months; where is there any text prescribing thirty-six months? Furthermore, unlined garments do not involve a period of seven months. Master Ying erred first in this regard, and subsequent scholars blindly followed this fallacious theory without examining it." Liu Ban stated: "The mourning attire instituted by Emperor Wen was strictly reckoned from the time after the burial took place. Prior to the burial, mourners wore untrimmed sackcloth <term>zhancui</term>. For the various emperors of Han, the time from demise to burial frequently exceeded one hundred days; so long as the burial had not taken place, mourning garments were not shed. In the biography of Zhai Fangjin, when his stepmother died, he returned to attend to official business thirty-six days after her burial had been completed; this serves as proof. Commentators who subsequently claimed this was substituting days for months were likewise misguided."</note>

<summary>Emperor Wen's testamentary edict establishes strict parameters for palace wailing and defines mourning attire periods lasting thirty-six days after burial, prompting detailed commentary on whether this abbreviated mourning substituted days for months.</summary>
